E1320.summary: The field where, in Atwood's figure, the Prototypes of the sacrificial beasts remain feeding and fattening; the text does not explain it further.
E1320.body: Atwood speaks of the sacrificial beasts “whilst their Prototypes remain feeding and fattening in the Philosophic Field” [III.2 ¶44]. The passage gives no further explanation of the expression.

E1321.summary: The realm whose powers, Atwood says, are shaken and defiled during the putrefaction.
E1321.body: In Atwood's account of the putrefaction, “the powers of the Philosophic Heaven are so wonderfully shaken and defiled” [III.1 ¶58]. The text does not define the Philosophic Heaven further here.

E1322.summary: The subject of the Hermetic work: hidden in the central motion of mineral life, called by many names, properly the Stone in concrete form, and described as an excruciated ens of Light.
E1322.body:
Atwood treats the philosophic matter as the subject of the work. It lies hidden “in the central motion of the mineral life, where the spirit is first coagulated and conceives itself into a concrete form” [I.3 n13]. It has many names: she notes one author who “eloquently identifies the philosophic matter, calling it mens sublimes et mare patens” (a mind sublime, and an open sea) [I.3 n13], and says that “in the concrete form, and for reasons before given in part, it has been properly called the Stone” [I.3 n16].

In Part IV she describes it as “the philosophic matter, drawn in part from the heterogeneous air and defiled breath of vitality” [IV.1 ¶46], which is purified into an immortal Form of Light. She mentions that Basil Valentine goes on to describe it after the passage she quotes (“before proceeding to a description of the Philosophic Matter” [III.2 ¶19]), but that description is not given there.

Quoted voices: in Hermes, the Son bears the Matter, which has a fixed watery form; the Master says “For this Son is the treasury, bearing even (in his hand) the Philosophic Matter” [IV.2 ¶14].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood gives two definitions: “The Philosophic Matter is an excruciated ens of Light”, “alight extracted through anguish from Life” [APP ¶84]; and “The Philosophical matter is the entelechy of body bearing the spirit” [APP ¶178].

Asserted identities: = the Stone [I.3 n16]; = mens sublimes et mare patens [I.3 n13]; = excruciated ens of Light [APP ¶84]; = entelechy of body bearing the spirit [APP ¶178].

E1323.summary: In the Appendix, being conversant with the soul in her philosophy: the recreative, or rather separative, process.
E1323.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood glosses the philosophic process as being “conversant with the soul in her philosophy --- i.e., the recreative, or rather separative, process” [APP ¶181].

E1324.summary: A figure in the Art whose will, unlike natural species, is free to form itself about its own self-multiplicative Light; the text does not define it directly.
E1324.body: Atwood writes that “the will of the philosophic Proteus is free to be drawn without hindrance” [I.2 ¶48]. Unlike natural species, it is free to form itself about its own self-multiplicative Light. The context apparently ties it to the fermented Vital Spirit, but the passage does not define it.

E1325.summary: A Salt discovered in the work, glossed as the voluntary bond; its solution is the Second Work, and knowing it is the secret of the Ancient Sages.
E1325.body:
Atwood says that the stated periods of the work are often metaphorical: “the periods are often to be understood metaphorically with respect to the discovery of the philosophic Salt” [IV.1 ¶17]. She glosses it as the voluntary bond, writing of “the Solution of the Philosophic Salt (i.e., the voluntary bond)” [IV.1 ¶36]. This solution is the Second Work, and “He who knows the Salt and its solution, knows the secret of the Ancient Sages.” [IV.1 ¶37].

Asserted identity: = the voluntary bond [IV.1 ¶36].

E1326.summary: The Matter considered as the subject of the work: universal, with perfective virtues, burdened with superfluities, and prepared by slow, gentle, continuous trituration.
E1326.body:
Atwood uses the term for the Matter as the subject on which the work is done. She speaks of “the alleged virtue and perfective properties of the Philosophic Subject” [I.2 ¶34], which go beyond ordinary light phenomena, and calls it universal, so that every epithet fits it: “inasmuch as nothing can be said amiss of a Universal Subjet” [I.2 ¶37].

She defers its full treatment, saying the mystical death and regeneration will become clearer “when we come to treat of the manifestation of the Philosophic Subject” [II.3 ¶56]. The ass's qualities are “very applicable and necessary to be found in the Philosophic Subject” [III.2 ¶64] if it is to carry out the Divine behests.

In Part IV the subject is prepared by hand (“Preparation of the Philosophic Subject” [IV.1 ¶2]). It is burdened with “such a mass of heterogeneous superfluities adhering to our subject” [IV.1 ¶7], and is worked by “the trituration of the Philosophic Subject, which ought to be slow, gentle, and continuous” [IV.1 ¶13].

E1327.summary: The vessel of the work, concealed by Hermes, described as having an apparatus of nerves, veins and alembics, and best when it accords with the vessel of nature.
E1327.body:
Atwood notes that “Hermes has chosen to conceal the philosophic vessel” [I.3 n48]. The context places the science in all bodies and its preparation in the innermost chamber of life.

Later she describes “the Philosophic Vessel and its multiform distillatory apparatus, of nerves, veins, and alembics” [III.4 ¶30]. The best vessel is “She that concordeth with vessel of nature” [III.4 ¶31]. It is finally constructed and vitrified by the Spirit and is called 'oracular'. The described apparatus apparently suggests a vessel within the living body, but the records do not state this directly.

E1328.summary: The one water from which all things grow and into which they dissolve, containing its own sulfur; Hermes' Aqua Philosophica that dissolves the elements.
E1328.body:
Atwood speaks of things “which have their growth all from the same identical water, and are resolved into the same again” [I.3 n5]. This water is divided into four relations and contains its own sulfur: “this water or mercury of the adepts has, within itself, its own good sulfur” [I.3 n5].

In the voice of Hermes it is addressed: “O, blessed watery pontic form, that dissolvest the elements” [I.3 ¶27]. Its dissolution of the composition is the key of restoration. Atwood's note on this passage adds: “Great is the reputed virtue of this Aqua Philosophica, which distills itself finally to manifestation by the Art of Life” [I.3 n36]. It cleanses inwardly and itself, and, joined in consciousness with the central Efficient, becomes the key of every magic art. It is learned only by practice.

Asserted identity: = mercury of the adepts [I.3 n5].

E1329.summary: The work proper, begun only after right motive and complete purification, with a threefold order of operation concealed by the Adepts and distinct from the preliminary practice.
E1329.body:
Zachary, as quoted, advises reading the philosophers and praying “before thou extendest thy Hand to the Philosophic Work” [III.4 ¶20]. An unclear voice equates the work with the practice: “the practice (that is of the ultimate Philosophic Work)” [III.4 ¶44].

Atwood says “few are chosen to proceed with the Philosophic Work” [IV.1 ¶31] out of those who consult on the means. It begins only after the right Motive, complete mundification and crystalline diaphaneity, so that only then can it be said “that the Philosophic Work has been said truly to being” [IV.1 ¶48]. Everything before is preparatory. She supports this with verse: “The philosopher’s worke doe not begin Till all things be pure without and within” [IV.1 ¶49].

Part IV.2 is headed “Of the Philosophic or Subtle Work” [IV.2 ¶1]. There Atwood says that “in the Philosophic Work, preceding her, there is a threefold order of legitimate operation” [IV.2 ¶3], which the Adepts concealed. Norton's verse calls it 'this Subtill Werke'.

Asserted identities: = Subtle Work [IV.2 ¶1]; = the practice [III.4 ¶44].

E1330.summary: A process out of which the Matter first appears pure and white; the text does not explain it further.
E1330.body: Atwood reports that the Matter comes forth “pure, as they say, and white, out of the philosophical contrition” [I.2 ¶36]. The term is not further explained there.

E1331.summary: In the Appendix, the dissolution in which soul and spirit separate from the breathless body, held to it as by a thread until refixation.
E1331.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “In the Philosophical dissolution of the body, soul and spirit are separate” [APP ¶96]. They remain joined to the breathless body as by a thread until refixation.

E1332.summary: A product of the work whose divine virtues wise men admire; things altered by the pure mineral spirit come to equal it.
E1332.body: Atwood mentions “the Philosophical Elixir, whose divine virtues wise men so much admire” [I.2 ¶49]. Things altered by the pure mineral spirit come to equal it. Nearby she separately names 'the elixir of the wise' as the result of superior skill and coction in vegetal life [I.2 ¶46]; the text does not say the two are the same.

E1333.summary: Reason's desire for its antecedent light.
E1333.body:
Atwood defines philosophy as reason's longing for its source: “philosophy was a desire of this kind, an appetition of reason for its antecedent light” [II.1 ¶44].

Asserted identity: = an appetition of reason for its antecedent light [II.1 ¶44].

E1334.summary: A piece in Ashmole's collection that Atwood counts among the most instructive.
E1334.body: Atwood lists *Philosophy and Experience* among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole's collection [I.1 ¶64].

E1335.summary: In quoted verse, the bright appearance that follows the blackness and its strange colours, and the coming God whom only the pure can endure.
E1335.body: The term appears in quoted verse. Bloomfield, as quoted, says that after the blackness and its strange colours, “Then shall Phoebus appear first out” [IV.2 ¶36], signalling the joy to come. In the hymn (Callimachus) Phoebus is the coming God whom only the pure endure: “Bright Phoebus comes and thunders at the gate.” [IV.2 ¶38]. In context this apparently marks the light that follows the dark stage of the work.

E1336.summary: Atwood's figure for something with a reviviscent spirit that passed from East to West, apparently alchemy; in a quoted source, the deep red bird that appears after the fire.
E1336.body:
Atwood writes that “our Phoenix too bestirred herself, and passed into the West” [I.1 ¶37], around the twelfth century, and gives it a 'reviviscent spirit'. The context suggests the Phoenix here stands for alchemy itself, but this is an inference.

Cornelius Agrippa's ingenious disciple, as quoted, describes the Phoenix that appears after the fire is fortified: “It is a red bird of a most deep color with a shining fiery hue.” [III.1 ¶50]. It is fed with the fire of its father as meat and the ether of its mother as drink.

E1337.summary: Medicine as Crollius describes it: a knowledge to be tried by fire, inseparable from pyrotechny, and practised by the physician.
E1337.body: Crollius, as quoted, says “the trial of the knowledge of physic is to be made by fire” [III.1 ¶10]. In his account physic cannot be separated from pyrotechny, and it is practised by the 'physician'.

E1338.summary: Atwood's two divergent kinds of science, physical (external, sensory, utilitarian) and moral (inward); neither can prove or disprove the other, and the Hermetic Science would include both.
E1338.body: Atwood contrasts the two. The Physical sciences rest on an external basis, take the senses as evidence and practical utility as their end. The Moral sciences have their evidence and object within the mind and slight worldly benefits. The two diverge, with “the Spiritual unable to prove itself absolutely, or the Material to disprove the other practically” [IV.4 ¶11]. The Hermetic Science would include both.

E1339.summary: Kirchberger's term, endorsed by Atwood: making the invisible spirit visible, by taking the infinite Light-nature into bound through hypostatic multiplication of its image.
E1339.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood adopts Kirchberger's term. The physical problem is “the making visible the invisible spirit” [APP ¶93]: taking the infinite Light-nature into bound by hypostatic multiplication of its image.

E1340.summary: The Art whose 'obstetric hand' assists the Stone's own regenerative self-manifestation.
E1340.body: In the words of the mysterious adeptest, the Stone is “made manifest by itself regeneratively by the obstetric hand of the Physico-Chemical Art” [III.3 ¶50]. The Art apparently assists, as a midwife does, a manifestation the Stone accomplishes itself.

E1341.summary: A writer whose De Auro Atwood cites to link Alchemy with profound metaphysics and to report a friend making gold and silver in his presence.
E1341.body: Picus di Mirandola is named in a list of authorities [I.1 ¶39]. Atwood cites his *de Auro* (*Opus Aureum de Auro*) to support the link of Alchemy with profound metaphysical science [I.1 ¶64, I.1 n69]. She also cites *De Auro* for his testimony that a friend made gold and silver in his presence: “I have seen it and done it myself” [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n103]. Atwood uses him as a supporting witness.

E1342.summary: A writer on the Elixir in Ashmole's collection whom Atwood cites on the Matter and the Stone, and on the piety needed by the seeker.
E1342.body:
Atwood names Pierce the Black Monk among the 'ecclesiastics of different orders' who agree concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. She counts his *Fragment* among the most instructive pieces in Ashmole's collection [I.1 ¶64].

From his verses on the Elixir she quotes a recipe for the Stone with the Water of Might: “In Arsenic sublimed there is a way straight” [III.3 ¶16, III.3 n6]. From the same work in Ashmole's *Theatr.* she takes support for the view that the subject is a seed from a body, not common gold and silver. The seeker must be pious, charitable and prayerful, and covetous men never find it: “Therefore there ys no other waye But to take thee to thy beades and pray:” [III.4 ¶21, III.4 n23]. Atwood cites him in support.

E1343.summary: A philosopher Atwood cites widely, for veiled hyperphysical philosophy, self-knowledge, philosophic death, intellectual intuition and the Matter; she declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher.
E1343.body:
Atwood cites Plato many times, almost always in support.

**Veiled philosophy.** From many dialogues and Epistle II she takes his hyperphysical, veiled philosophy and his dread of writing the truth: “it is a parturition respecting this ingenerated in the soul, from which he who is not liberated will never in reality acquire truth” [I.1 ¶17, I.1 n23]. She suggests the science behind it was practical but declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher. She mentions him as translated by Ficinus [I.1 ¶64]. She also places him in the 'golden chain of Hermetic philosophers' who traced the poets' allusions and claimed Homer and Virgil as their own [III.1 ¶25].

**Self-knowledge and the Mysteries.** From the *First Alcibiades*: “to know oneself is Wisdom and the highest virtue of the soul” [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n33]; he “calls the magic of Zoroaster the service of the gods” [II.1 ¶51]. From the *Phaedo*: assimilation through the Greater Mysteries and the divine eye, “better worth than 10,000 corporeal eyes” [II.2 ¶5, II.2 ¶8], and philosophic death, “it is the business of philosophers to study how to be dead” [II.3 ¶37]. Wisdom belongs to old age, meaning intuitive Intellect free of imaginative error; he condemns 'two-fold ignorance' [II.2 ¶13].

**Descent and ascent.** “It is necessary that a man should have his right opinion as firm as adamant in him when he descends into Hades” [II.3 ¶12]. He likens the soul's descent into generation to an earthquake [II.3 ¶20], and compares Glaucus deformed by weeds to the viscous soul [II.3 ¶30]. On intuition: “on a sudden a light, as it were a leaping fire, will be enkindled in the soul, and will there itself nourish itself” [II.3 ¶50]. Pure souls see visions “resident in a Pure Light” [II.4 ¶29]. “Plato beautifully unfolds the passive method of the Divine Intuition” [II.4 ¶40] through love, hope and faith. Atwood reads his “there are many more thrysus bearers than Bacchic souls” [II.4 ¶54] as meaning that many have the fire but cannot draw it forth.

**The Matter.** He places earth within heaven: he “calls it the most ancient element within the heaven” [III.2 ¶36]. Matter is grasped “by a sort of defective or ablative reasoning” [III.2 ¶53]. The *Timaeus* is read as alluding to the Etheral Quintessence [III.2 ¶38], and “the Quintessence of Plato” is identified with the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. Via Olympiodorus his Tartarus is read ethically, physically and psychically [III.2 ¶9], and via Proclus the Meadow is the prolific power of life [II.4 ¶16].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is cited for alchemy being understood only by those “conversant with the soul in her philosophy” [APP ¶181].

E1345.summary: A late Platonic writer Atwood cites for Sacred Arts replacing lost revelation, an exhortation to inner stillness, and the soul's ascent from image to Archetype.
E1345.body: Atwood cites the Platonic Successor, via Iamblichus on the Mysteries and Taylor's notes, for the view that Sacred Arts replace lost spontaneous revelation: “has given us observation through Sacred Arts, by which we have at hand sufficient assistance” [II.1 ¶53, II.1 n46]. She praises the 'magnificence of thought and diction' of his exhortation to inner stilling and adoration of the First: “Now, if ever, to remove from ourselves multiform knowledge” [II.4 ¶41]. She also cites him on the soul's ascent from image to Archetype and its recovery after falling from the vision of God: “he will again, says the Platonic Successor, be elevated” [III.3 ¶26]. In every case she endorses him.

E1346.summary: The later Platonists, whose 'highly elevated philosophy' Atwood says agrees in the same divine tradition.
E1346.body: Atwood cites the Platonic successors to show that their 'highly elevated philosophy' agrees in the same divine tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

E1347.summary: Cited by Atwood as agreeing with the doctrine of primitive non-being.
E1347.body: Atwood cites Platonic theology as agreeing with the doctrine of primitive non-being [III.2 ¶33].

E1348.summary: Paired voices Atwood cites for the view that the First Matter is unknown, or known only as nothing.
E1348.body: Atwood cites the Platonist and the Kabalist together for the view that the First Matter is unknown, or is known as nothing [III.2 ¶57].

E1349.summary: The Platonic school, cited by Atwood for the whiteness of true Being, the origin of matter, the Epic Cycle as a secret of creation, and the Mysteries as Initia.
E1349.body: Atwood cites the Platonists in support: “The Platonists have declared true Being to be white” [III.2 ¶9], and she draws on their view of the origin of matter [III.2 ¶9]. She reports them as saying that the Epic Cycle includes the true philosophic secret of creation [III.3 ¶42]. 'The Platonist' is cited again for the Mysteries having been called Initia [II.2 ¶4]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she contrasts them with Behmen: the Platonists are more scientific and less descriptive [APP ¶62].

E1350.summary: Author of the Hist. Nat., whom Atwood cites on Ostanes bringing the Persian spirit to Greece, Democritus' fame and occult practice, and Caligula's failed attempts.
E1350.body: Atwood cites Pliny's *Hist. Nat.* (lib. xxx, cap. I; lib. 33, cap. 4) in support of three points: Ostanes brought the Persian spirit to Greece; Democritus was famous for experiment and practised in secret; and Caligula's attempts failed [I.1 ¶12, I.1 ¶18, I.1 n13, I.1 n17, I.1 n26]. She quotes: “Plenum miraculi et hoc pariter utrasque artes effloruisse, medicinam dico, magiciemque eadem aetate” (our rendering: this too is full of wonder, that both arts flourished together, medicine, I mean, and magic, in the same age) [I.1 ¶12].
